Would try again!
May 2016 • Friends
Hu Tieu is pho's less popular little brother. The broth is more delicate and the cuts of meat are a bit different.

"Nam Vang" means Phnom Penh style meaning this particular Hu Tieu noodle soup uses Cambodian style spices and garnishes. You have the choice of dry noodles with soup on the side or soup in the noodles. I opted for the dry style which tasted similar to Indonesian Mi Goreng. Take a few bites and slurp the broth on the side like a drink. My meal was very satisfying, but at the same time, I wasn't Wowed by the meal overall.

I definitely would try it again with the broth in the noodles instead for a different take on the restaurant.

Amazing Cambodian noodles, open 24 hours
Dec 2016 • Couples
This place has "Nam Vang" (Vietnamese for Phnom Penh) noodles, and it's so well known that people from other cities in Vietnam road-trip at night (it's open 24 hours) to eat here. We found out about it from the Eat Saigon book (Elly Nguyen) that goes on about how famous this restaurant is. The noodles are slightly chewy and hard, not too soft, and are served with shrimp and a bunch of organ meats that you don't have to eat. 

You can get the noodles "nuoc" (in broth) or "kho" (dry, broth on the side). I think they taste much better dry, and you can drink the broth on the side.

They do speak basic English here, but there's really nothing to talk about... not many options, just order and eat. Not cheap, about 80,000, but worth it. Oh, and really, Hu Tieu Nam Vang is the only dish here... we saw the table next to ours trying to order pho. No pho here.
